subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS ACT, 1975 MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT PORTS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after waiting for 15 days and repeatedly attacking the government to inform it about an exceedingly serious situation in the province of Quebec, especially as concerns feed grain supplies for farm producers, the government has finally understood that the situation is truly urgent, even after negating this urgency.
I remember that in all good faith, all hon. members asked many questions, sometimes to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), sometimes to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in relation with the consequences of the longshoremen's strike in Quebec ports.
I understand that the ministers did not have to give us all the information that they had when we asked our questions, but I also understand that Parliament must be kept informed as much as possible about situations which interest the whole population, whether they affect producers or consumers.
I have always thought that a government exists in a society to put order when problems are caused by conflicts between the various categories of persons, associations or workers of a country. And I have never thought that when the government acts, it is by introducing an oppressive measure concerning one class instead of another.
I do not believe that the bill now introduced by the Minister of Labour falls into this category. It is an extreme measure, aimed at finding a solution to allow the continuity of a production required by Canadians and to prevent considerable losses for several types of farm producers who are fed up because they cannot get supplies.
On April 9, Madam Speaker, because I was aware of this situation and had received many telegrams from farm producers and their associations in the province of Quebec, I had taken it upon myself to present a motion under the terms of Standing Order 26 to ask for an emergency debate. The Chair had decided to adjourn the holding of such a debate.
However, the situation having deteriorated in the following days, I returned to the charge on April 16 with a similar motion, at which time the Chair decreed an emergency sitting.
During that debate, Madam Speaker, I endeavoured to show what the situation really was, even to the extent of quoting authentic figures on the quantities of feed grains available at the elevators in the port of Quebec City. At that time I refrained from quoting figures on Trois-Rivieres or Montreal elevators, because there was no need for it. There was no way feedmills could get into both ports and have their supplies in a normal way.
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is not here, but anyway if my remarks do not agree with the information published in newspapers, I know beforehand that he will correct remarks published by the press.
Labour Dispute
Since he was not present at the outset of the April 16 debate, newspapers reported that the Minister of Agriculture said this:
An emergency debate never moved grain.
I also know that such a debate never moved grain. Every member knows that. Such was not the aim of the debate, but rather to allow those moving it to have access to the ports and to obtain that longshoremen fulfill their duties, discharge their responsibilities by unloading the ships and loading the elevators.
In view of the serious situation prevailing, I thought we had a duty to act in that way. I realize more than ever that we were right in so doing. Not only did we draw the government's attention, but we also gave hope to people, organizations and farmers victimized by the situation.
Today, on this 23rd of April, the situation is no better. I suspect the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) must have been informed. Right at this time, there is in Quebec City's elevators 48,000 bushels of wheat, 45,000 of oats, 48,000 of barley, 396,000 of corn. That does not mean that every teamster, every miller coming to Quebec City's port will have its truck loaded with grain. This grain belongs to a few millers, Out of the hundred, two or three only can get their supplies. They could do so, as a matter of fact, but they no longer can since the checkers have also gone on strike. The latter struck and are now keeping the trucks owned by the millers from picking up their grain in the port of Quebec City. The situation is even worse than that. They even stop the owners of the feed grains from picking up their own feed, their own property.
On the other hand, a grain barge entered the port of Quebec. The grain handlers are unloading it, just the way it is done on the black market. This is no joke: in Canada, right in the port of Quebec City, the oldest port on the North American continent, labourers are forced to work as if we were at war, on the sly, as if for a black market. And that goes on in 1975! That means the situation is extremely serious. In this case we are concerned with supplying the domestic market. The longshoremen have nothing to do with that, not even normally. They are there to unload the ships, the ocean liners. In the case of barges that transport goods for the Canadian market, it is not up to them to load or unload them. In this case, we are dealing with grain handlers. They perform their work with great difficulty. We are left then with trucking. The former speaker, a while ago, mentioned the possibility of transport by truck or by rail.
I would like to give some particulars on the great transport opportunities by truck or by rail and the supplies needed in Quebec and then we could see whether it is urgent for Parliament to pass that bill.
According to the information that I obtained today, it is related to a question asked yesterday in Quebec City to the Minister of Agriculture. On April 22, the Minister of Agriculture stated in answer to a question that 150 railway cars reach the province of Quebec every day.
We went to the sources of information and checked further. It was revealed that in the last nine days, a daily average of 48 cars-a far cry from 150-were dispatched to the ports of Quebec, each car containing some 2,000 bushels or a maximum of 2,500 bushels.

April 23, 1975
Labour Dispute
Two injunctions were therefore requested by the Trois-Rivieres Feed Mill Owners Association. The injunctions were not obeyed. Since the volume of grain moved is not as told, injunctions are sought to get supplies from a port where there is an abundance of grain; according to my information, there are actually in the port of Trois-Rivieres, 1,300,000 bushels awaiting takers. A large quantity of those 1,300,000 bushels belong to feed mill owners, grain that was bought in December or January, that is ready for delivery but out of reach.
This morning, on April 23, again in the province of Quebec, the port was exceptionally crowded; even taxis could not pick up passengers arriving on other ships. That means people were coming and going in the port, but the movement was not such as to allow farm producers and feed mill owners to get grain supplies.
The weekly consumption of feed grain in the province of Quebec amounts to 2 million bushels. One can readily appreciate the predicament in which Quebec producers are. They are concerned, and duly so.
We can read in newspapers that feed grain shortages causing irreparable wrong to Quebec livestock producers. Some people think that we are joking, that hogs could never eat one another. That is quite normal. When there is not enough food to go around, all hogs in the pig sty will fight and the big ones will eat the small ones. That is the normal way for hogs to behave in society; we must call things by their names.
However, when reasonable men who are endowed with intelligence, judgment and experience are behaving exactly the same way, I say this is unacceptable! Well, if such things are unacceptable, we must take steps to prevent them, for they must not occur. To prevent that, we must ensure the sound distribution of goods and of whatever is required for production and consumption. I think that it is the duty of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) to find a temporary solution. However, while temporary, I would not like that solution to be a drawback for the workers. I understand the workers have rights but they also do wrong, just as we do in certain other areas of society. It must be understood that we have rights andthat sometimes we do wrong when we do not fulfill all our responsibilities.
So the government's role is to keep a lookout, to check what exactly is going on in every field of human endeavour, so that we respect each other, so that we act like men do, like intellegent men do. I would not like to read in the newspapers tomorrow or the day after that the hon. member for Bellechasse or still Parliament have declared war on workers. Absolutely not! I respect the right to strike as a fundamentel one. It is endorsed by law. But when it is time for a collective agreement to be renewed, when we fail to come to an agreement and when talks are dragging on, then it is imperative that an authority intervene and try to conciliate disagreeing parties and see to it that lengthy discussions do not cause considerable damage to other workers in the same society.
It is in this spirit that Parliament must consider today's legislation to which we did not have the opportunity to give much consideration because we just received it, along

with the report of Judge Gold, conciliation commissioner. We have had precious little time to study it. Still parliamentarians should not be expected to perform miracles, to try to become acquainted with a bill or a document before they receive it. One must be reasonable. I surely hope that during the procedure in committee of the whole the minister and his officials will be in a position to answer the questions that will be put to them by members so that, if necessary, amendments can be made to the bill so as to make it fair and efficient.
Madam Speaker, this morning someone asked me why the Agricultural Producers' Union-which, all things considered, is a labour union-did not itself take an injunction against longshoremen in the ports of Quebec City, Trois-Rivieres and Montreal. I think that might have been possible. I think that might have given results a little sooner. But let us imagine ourselves in their shoes-workers against workers coming face to face. They both have rights, they both have obligations. So, in a given situation there is a confrontation and one of the two unions asks the court for an injunction to prevent the other from exercising its right to strike. Such situations are extremely difficult. I do not say it is impossible but I do say it is difficult and I think that although it is difficult it might have been normal to try that procedure, not to place those people in conflict, a potentially dangerous confrontation, but to test our policies in such a situation because I think for my part that, to my knowledge, it is the first time such a thing occurs.
Given the gravity of the situation, associations, particularly the APU, turned to Parliament. Will we, parliamentarians, try to turn to others to avoid our responsabilities? I say no. I say we must take our responsibilities because the interest of the whole community is at stake.
During the weekend I saw with my own eyes 36 calves killed, hooked on a cable along a road because they cannot be delivered on the market, nobody wants to buy them. Everything is disorganized, and the ravens will eat that meat, and this fall people will not be able to buy meat.
But if this is a recurring situation, it means that we shall be wasting a possible production which might be needed in six or eight months. Same thing with respect to egg production. We heard about eggs at length last year. We even had a special committee of the House which met a number of times to study egg marketing. Well, if this situation is allowed to go on, I think they will no longer have to have special meetings on egg marketing, for considering the number of hens sent to the slaughterhouse for want of feed, I guess the problem of egg overproduction or marketing will no longer arise. And we have the same situation in respect of poultry meat.
Now, with respect to all those equally serious questions, even if it hurts, even if we may be somewhat unpopular for a while, even if we give workers the impression that we are passing legislation to force them to do something against their will, I answer that when we think back upon it, after we have had the advantage of analysing every situation, we will all agree that those measures were necessary and even in the interest of workers.
I wish us to have the common weal in mind throughout this debate. I personally do not want to accuse anybody. I do not hold anybody responsible for the present situation,
April 23, 1975

but I will hold our Parliament and government responsible tomorrow and on the following days if, in the light of the situations we are witnessing, we do not amend our labour code so as to have a permanent mechanism at our disposal to make conciliation and the renewal of collective agreements easier, instead of allowing situations to deteriorate. We should heed from day to day the progression and the way of looking at things, the way workers put their claims, and the way employers answer workers' demands. Workers are not the only ones involved, Madam Speaker, there are also numbers of heartless employers, people who do not want to admit that they should not operate only to make profits, but that consideration should also be given to services to be provided to people. We must admit that those who contribute to assure these services or to produce this or that product also have rights and that these rights must be recognized. The employers are not sensible enough to recognize them in practice. It is therefore the government's duty-and Parliament's duty, since it is the supreme authority in this country-to pass legislation which will force these heartless organizations to be more reasonable.
I heard today on the radio a statement of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) on cartels and large corporations, and I understood that a commission would be formed to study what goes on in that field and that the government will also introduce legislation establishing the regulations these cartels and large corporations will have to comply with. I hope it is true, but I would not want another inefficient piece of legislation. We have the anti-combines and anti-cartel acts, but they are practically never enforced, and the penalties are so small that when the companies that openly violate these acts are convicted, they do not care a bit about justice because the penalties are so small.
We need a sharp-edged legislation, so that when a corporation is sued for having violated the law, for having abused the public or for having made excessive profits to the detriment of workers, the legislation will be enforced to teach a good lesson to the others who would be tempted to do the same. That is called an efficient Parliament, a government which is aware of its responsibilities and which is willing to assume them.
One must not only create the impression that something is being done, that legislation is being passed, but those laws must not become a dead letter. We must have operative and effective laws upon which all Canadians may rely. So I hope that once this bill is passed we do not remain idle saying that everything has been done. No, we will have to work to improve bargaining conditions in all areas so as to avoid those strikes that plague this country. It is discouraging. It has come to the point where people are worrying about the future, asking themselves what is going to happen or whether such or such service will be working.
We do not live within a stable society. And such an unstable society involves small cells of disruption. Those who set up cells are allowed to disrupt society, to organize revolution without admitting it but through very active means. We give them tools without knowing it. To govern
Labour Dispute
is to foresee, to look after the common good as far as it is humanly possible to do so.
I believe that in such a situation, we will take the trouble of scrutinizing the law. That cannot be perfect, it is made by men and therefore can be changed by men. We will try to scrutinize the law to see if it is really effective. Are we going to do injustice to a given class of people? Is it worth while doing so, so as to progress and enable other classes of people, of producers to keep on playing their part? It seems to me there are enough problems nowadays in the agricultural field and that we should not create any more. Now it is in that spirit that I address myself to this bill and I am sure that if we all get together and try to make this legislation into the best possible law, nobody will be dissatisfied and a great step will be taken on the road to social, economic and political stability in this country.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS ACT, 1975 MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT PORTS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate today. May I say right off to the hon. minister responsible that we will support, without hesitating his bill which finally meets with the wish expressed over a week ago.
I must also congratulate the hon. members who took part in the debate, bearing in mind their information and intentions. We support this bill which we feel is most urgent. To my mind, it is the totally logical result of the special debate held last week.
Madam Speaker, I know some hon. members may have found me severe, and I said so last week. I was not the happiest of men when I moved my motion, as did the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), even though it had the support of my colleagues.
I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the hon. members on both sides of the House who took part in the debate last week. Generally speaking, I believe that we have discussed this problem sufficiently to make the government understand the importance of resolving it and the difficulties which the farmers are facing.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), replying on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture who is justifiably absent, had accused us of suggesting this debate for unfounded or illogical reasons. The hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bech-ard) has already started to interrupt me, but I shall forgive him since I know that this is one of his habits.
Last week, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said that our debate was unfounded, but I believe that today, the Minister of Labour, by the decision that he made, has replied very objectively to our invitation and that of all hon. members who were asking last week that the government take its responsibilities.
It is certain that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs found that we could not offer any answers, but the answer that we requested last week is the same that we request everyday from the government-that it take its responsibilities. This is what the minister is doing today. The government has some authority and, in view of the situation, it is finally replying to our invitation of last week.

April 23, 1975
Labour Dispute
Madam Speaker, I must also point out that a government member had the courage to talk about the need for special legislation. I am speaking about the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), who made an excellent speech last week. We recognize this and I believe that he had already foreseen a solution. And one can wonder why we have waited so long, and what are the possibilities to right the wrongs.
Certainly some members are still convinced that the farmers did not lose anything, that they did not have any difficulty. Maybe they should read from time to time the news releases from the APU president and other representatives of the millers association and, especially, from the farmers themselves, to realize the enormous difficulties the latter have met.
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) told us the numerous difficulties he noted in his riding last weekend. I think all hon. members from rural ridings know that full well.
We therefore had valid reason to request concrete action from the government and today, we wholeheartedly responded in the affirmative to a legislation which, on the one side, will not be accepted right away by the workers of this sector, but, on the other side, corresponds to a real need.
We regret being forced to favour the implementation of such a measure, taking into account the workers, but, even then, I wonder to what extent we must say that nobody is responsible.
To my mind, contrary to what the hon. member for Bellechasse said earlier, there are responsible people and, as member of this House, as representatives, \ye have responsibilities to take on both sides of the House. Our present duty is to ask the government for immediate measures. That is what we are doing, and I think our responsibility then is part of the commitment we all took in our ridings.
I wish to say, Madam Speaker, that the government through this emergency measure presented today is answering our questions. We have been asking questions for three weeks. The government is taking a responsibility for which we have been calling for three weeks. I believe it is important that not only government members but also the whole labour sector concerned know that we have been demanding this measure for the sake of 6,000 egg producers. It was also for the sake of 15,000 poultry and turkey producers. We did it for 23,000 industrial milk producers, 5,000 fluid milk producers and 6,000 hog producers, as well as for all Quebec consumers, millions of them, who were waiting and calling for concrete government action. I think we are indeed meeting a big enough need of the community.
Therefore, all the feed supply in Quebec was, for all practical purposes, interrupted, breeding was in a difficult situation and egg producers would once again become the victims of American imports. Many of them would face bankruptcy. There was a rush on slaughterhouses and the food market would also be disturbed. Our farm producers support the consequences of a sixth strike within a year.

We had the strike of pilots, railway workers, inspectors, handlers, labourers and, today, longshoremen.
The situation is, and already was two weeks ago, dramatic and all the more abominable that agriculture in Quebec knows one of the worst crisis of its history, and rely on supplies of feed for more than 60 per cent to feed cattle.
The temporary measures of the government which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) pretended to be efficient last Wednesday, have proved completely unsatisfactory for three weeks because they were too late, too slow and too expensive.
Therefore, the government now recognizes the validity of our assertions and of the questions which all members in this House have put for three weeks. On both sides of the House, members felt it a duty to put some embarrassing questions to the minister; we now ask: How is it that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), or the Canadian Wheat Board, or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) did not give any answer to these repeated calls? Of course, it could be said that the guys in the opposition put questions so as to make headlines, and so on.
But there are still serious members on the other side of the House whose riding is affected. I was very happy to see those members show their interest in this area but, unfortunately, they did not get any answer. For three weeks, they did not come up with the answers we were expecting. I do not think that we could be reproached with not interfering. The Minister of Agriculture has been saying for three weeks that we were panicky, pessimistic, and that the information of the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), of the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) or, recently, the information of an NDP member, was not complete. There were many questions. The more we were trying to make the government aware of that alarming and dangerous situation, the more they answered us that it was untrue.
Last Wednesday, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was saying that supplies would last a month. Some were talking about half empty elevators. They did not say that access to the ports was impossible, and that regularly. Therefore faced with such positions, we were justified, I think, to ask for a special debate last week. Today, it is quite obvious that the opposition was right since the minister is forced to act now. Indeed just three days ago I was asking the Minister of Labour how negotiations were progressing, what news did the mediators report. Since April 2, we were told that negotiations were broken and that the time had not come to try to bring the two parties together again, no matter the situation in which the Quebec farmers found themselves.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, we were entirely right. It will surely be stated that we want again to play politics in this debate. I do not want to do so, but I want to remind those who have accepted parliamentary duties that they have failed to assume their responsibilities during the past few weeks. And we are pleased today, even if it will cost money, that the government has at last decided to take position.
Some members and even some ministers, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) for example, surely do not
April 23, 1975

relish the idea of passing an ad hoc legislation, they would still rather see the victims get a series of injunctions from the court. That, Madam Speaker, is either hypocrisy or perhaps artlessness, because the systematic resort to court injunctions is tantamount to the denial of the right to strike. We know that perfectly well, but we are afraid to say so. Last week, we were asked by the government members: "Tell us whether you are for or against the right to strike?"
Asking the question in those terms is much too easy, Madam Speaker. But we are all perfectly aware that as long as the government keeps urging companies to resort to injunctions, it renounces its responsibility to decide and act. "Well, let companies resort to injunctions". Yes, but it means for all practical purposes doing away with the right to strike.
So, the government decided to get rid of its reponsibili-ties and turn them over to the courts. Courts will settle the problem. The worse of this business, Madam Speaker, is that the labour movement once again used farmers to force the government to give in, while the government used ship owners to curb labour demands. All during that time, Quebec farmers and-by way of consequence-consumers became the hostages of longshoremen as well as the Ottawa government, as my colleague the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) was saying last Wednesday.
We are already wondering whether these longshoremen will abide by the law, or whether, as some indicated as recently as this morning, they will oppose the will of Parliament.
I should like to remind these working men for whom we have great consideration and for whom we wish a fair treatment, I should like to remind the inspectors and longshoremen that the alternative is not, as some of their representatives have mentioned at a given moment, whether Parliament must first protect the hogs or the longshoremen. Such a solution, in my opinion, is far too simplistic. Such a position only goes to show the misgivings, and even the contempt, that some of our fellow citizens might have vis-a-vis our farmers.
I feel that the choice must be made at the following level. The rights of longshoremen must be recognized, of course, for instance security of employment and a minimum income for their work. No member of Parliament, in my opinion, is obstinate or hesitant in recognizing them such rights. But there are other workers.
The real victims throughout this conflict, Madam Speaker, are not the people of Bay Street or St. James Street: the real victims are the agricultural workers.
I believe the best thing those concerned in the conflict, that is the workers, could do for Workers' Day next May 1, would be to go back to work willingly. I hope that they do so for the sake of the farmers, whose job security and income are much more threatened than those of unionized workers.
However, the longshoremen should not be alone in suffering from the bad effects of their strike, which we recognize as legitimate and legal. Later, in committee of the whole, we shall ensure that there is greater job secu-
Labout Dispute
rity. There does not seem to be any now according to the Gold report.
If the longshoremen have to go back proudly to work tomorrow, the government, once this measure is passed, will have to consider that its role is not finished. I believe that this may be the most important aspect of this issue, Madam Speaker. Today, we are discussing a special measure. Unfortunately, we have waited for it too long, and the workers as well as the members of Parliament knew very well that the government would be pressured, conditioned and forced to take some action. Indeed, the minister said earlier that he did not want to make this a case of first choice. This is not the first time that we have to legislate. It is not a precedent, as the minister said a while ago, far from it, for the government to be forced to introduce special legislation.
But tomorrow, as concerns the farmers, for instance, what guarantee do we have that the Quebec farmers, and especially those in eastern Quebec, will be compensated for the losses they have suffered during this conflict. We know that for those who could not get any supplies, the loss was much greater. What guarantee do we have from the government that the farmers will not lose their necessary profits? What guarantee do we have that the government will eventually make provisions for permanent measures which will allow us to be better prepared for such situations in the future? These are questions which we hope the members of the government, and especially the minister, will answer during the minutes to come.
And above all I wish to join with every party concerned with the new system of collective agreement, since the current one does not satisfy anybody anymore. Of course people are afraid. Politically speaking, this is dangerous matter, a vote here, a vote there if we start contesting labour unions, current methods. Still, I believe we must fact the facts. We must have the courage to say that we are not satisfied, that currently things are going wrong in every area.
I think the government has a responsibility to meet with the unions and review the so-called right to strike. There is no question of taking away the right to strike without compensation, some security, certain safeguards ensuring a fair deal to workers. But how far must we go? Today members say: "We will vote this special legislation but we will not remove the right to strike". But I submit we will be forced to call other workers back to work. If we are not affecting the right to strike, what then are we doing now? Are we not again taking the right to strike away from workers? So, a mechanism that used to do the job does not seem to meet today's requirements. Strikes break out in increasing numbers, at what cost and with what economic disruption! How long is this going to last? We have asked labour union representatives whether the right to strike is not used as a common tool nowadays.
Considering consequences, how far do they go in the assessment and weighing of their actions? These are questions that every member asks himself, but we do not dare deal with the issue in public, because there is always the danger of displeasing one category, which would be quite dangerous come election time. If, to be elected, we have to remain silent on problems that call for our attention, on solutions we should be promoting to protect the common

The Gold report is fairly thick but I suspect both sides will accept, either willingly or grudgingly, most of the recommendations in the report, with the exception of the job security provision which is the most crucial issue in this dispute. I would like the minister to let us know why he cannot accept exactly the same as was provided in the case of Vancouver. There an arbitrator was appointed and his decision was binding on both sides. There are arguments against that situation as well, but at least we would not be legislating a contract in the kind of detail that is in the Gold report.
Unless I am mistaken in my reading and understanding of the Gold report, we are legislating all of the longshoremen in Three Rivers back to work with a guarantee of
1.200	hours. Under the previous agreement they had a guarantee of 1,480 hours. Even with the wage package that is in this legislation they will be no better off, and possibly will be worse off, than they were under the old agreement. If, in fact, Mr. Gold's report says that the overtime they work from Monday to Friday will be deducted from the
1.200	hours, they will be in an even worse position. Surely we can do no less than legislate these men back to work in a way whereby they will be no worse off than before.
I ask the minister what is wrong with these amendments? They do exactly what was done before, namely, leave it to an arbitrator to examine Mr. Gold's recommendations on job security. The only point we are trying to make is with regard to the job security issue. As far as I am concerned the other 60 or 70 pages of Mr. Gold's report can go "as is", with possibly only minor changes. After meeting with both sides surely an arbitrator will endeavour to meet these points and come up with something that is more acceptable with regard to job security provisions.
If we in this parliament insist on legislating men back to work in Three Rivers with a guarantee of 1,200 hours instead of 1,480 hours, and other men with a guarantee of 1,400 hours instead of the former 1,480 hours, even with the pay increase they could well lose if the overtime hours are counted against them. An officer of the union said that what has been given in the wage package, which is not too bad, has been taken away once or twice in the job security provisions of maximum hours guaranteed in the course of a year's work. I just cannot see workers of any kind sitting still for that. Why does the minister not agree we can and should do exactly the same as we did in the Vancouver legislation?

Madam Chairman, I will answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and then get to the questions asked by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
With regard to the precedents we are dealing with here, the legislation we had dealing with the west coast longshoremen was in a situation where there was not a commissioner appointed. There was no board chairman appointed. In that situation the parties asked that there be no commissioner and no board chairman. They wished to negotiate themselves. However, they were unsuccessful in doing so. There was no report on which to base any legislation. That is why we just extended the collective agreement and appointed an arbitrator.
In this situation we have a commissioner's report. He made firm recommendations in contractual language. This is similar to the situation we had with the grainhandlers' strike on the west coast. In that case, Dr. Perry was the single man commission. He recommended all the provisions of the collective agreement, put it in contractual language, and parliament legislated the Perry recommendations in total as the collective agreement. In that particular case the commissioner's report had the support of the employees. Parliament supported the government. I believe the members of the New Democratic Party supported that legislation and, as I indicated, so did the union.
Here we have an analogous situation. We have a commissioner's report by Judge Alan Gold. Again, it is highly thought of by both union and management. Both agreed to him in this particular role as commissioner. He has come down with a report in detail. All the recommendations are in contractual language. However, this time it is agreed to by the employers and not the employees. We are following the same course, but it happens to be the opposite side of the coin in so far as who agrees to it. There is our precedent.
I will now turn to some of the points raised by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. I might just indicate to him that what is recommended here in terms of job security is a job security study provision that has been plaguing the proper operation of this port for endless years. It has been studied by the most able man in this field, Judge Alan Gold. It is agreed that in industrial relations his ability is unquestioned. Equally important, his experience in industrial relations is practiced in the St. Lawrence ports.
I repeat that it is appropriate to recall that in 1968, as I indicated in my opening remarks, and again in 1971 Judge Gold was appointed chairman of the conciliation board which dealt with the complex and difficult longshoring problems. He is the one who dealt with this particular situation. With regard to the differential between Trois-Rivieres, Quebec City and Montreal, he had a special assignment by Professor Bellemare that also looked into this. The situation is that the traffic is not as heavy in Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City as in Montreal.
I would point out to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre that job security in Montreal is higher, 1,600 hours as opposed to 1,480 hours. Of the 2,200 longshoremen, 1,600 are in Montreal. Therefore the vast majority do benefit. The recommendations are based on the most solid expertise we could get.

Even if the government followed another course, and this is hypothetical, and decided we would do something along the lines recommended by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, appoint an arbitrator and extend the current collective agreement, it is very unlikely we could find an arbitrator of the competence of Alan Gold.
These are essentially the reasons why we are recommending action along these lines. Once we have decided to proceed along the lines of incorporating a commissioner's report as the collective agreement, we cannot change that. Some of us may not like one particular aspect and want it deleted. Others may want other aspects deleted. Before we know it the whole thing could collapse and we would not have a coherent, cogent collective agreement incorporated in our legislation.

Madam Chairman, I recognize the difficulty of the minister. In this bill he is essentially proposing that we follow the recommendations of Mr. Justice Gold. We do not question the ability of Mr. Justice Gold or his past experience, but we are wondering how this will actually work. The minister said that 1,600 to 2,200 workers work in Montreal. They are protected, of course, by the provision that they will be guaranteed 2,000 hours. But we are concerned about the 600 workers in Quebec City and the workers in Three Rivers. In the case of the latter, they will be guaranteed not more than 1,200 hours. That works out to a guarantee of 30 weeks' work and a gross income of $6 per hour, or $7,200 for the year. For a married man with a wife and two children, that amounts to less than the poverty level. I do not think the minister can be very happy about making that kind of proposal.
I suggest to the minister that if the workers in Three Rivers are guaranteed only 30 weeks, they will be entitled to 20 weeks' unemployment insurance benefits. That seems a very strange proposition for the government to make. The worker would be guaranteed 30 weeks' work in the industry, and if that is all the work there is they will be guaranteed 20 weeks' unemployment insurance benefits. They then become, not the responsibility of the industry to which they are tied as long as they work but the responsibility of the Canadian taxpayers. This would not be just for one year but on a permanent basis unless there is more work in Three Rivers than the minister seems to feel there is.
The situation in Quebec City, while a little better is really not much better. Instead of 30 weeks, the workers would be guaranteed 35 weeks' work. Surely the minister can come up with a better, more humane proposal than that contained in this bill.

Those members sitting in the back row opposite who supported that comment should wait until they have been around a little while and suffered the consequences of making a mistake about what they are doing here. It may all be a little humorous to a number of members opposite, but some of us who are concerned for labour and the rights of labour in Canada do not regard it as humorous. Rather than identify the individual to whom these remarks are directed-he is relatively new around here-I will let him get away with it for once.
The step we have taken tonight is not a very healthy one for this parliament. The minister himself has indicated that this was not the procedure he would like to find himself pursuing. I hope that is true of all of us. When the House of Commons finds itself called upon arbitrarily to settle the terms of a collective agreement between two parties, I think we ought seriously to review our procedures, not only those in Part V of the Canada Labour Code but those set out in other legislation dealing with relations between employers and employees.
I have reservations about this bill which go beyond the fact that we are dealing with the terms of a collective agreement. They concern the very nature of the relationship between the Maritime Employers Association, the longshoremen's associations and the Government of Canada. The government is not here with completely free hands. It is party to a guarantee to secure to the banks certain amounts of money-I think the total amount owed by the MEA is now some $18 million.
The people have a right to know what is being done in this chamber tonight. The situation is not without conflict, and this conflict arises when it becomes apparent to those who are familiar with the financial obligations undertaken by the government-obligations which must, I suppose, be honoured-that the government is committed to honouring a debt of the Maritime Employers Association. It is in the best interests of the government that this strike be settled. It is not necessarily in the best interests of the employers and members of the unions involved, save for one respect.
However, clearly there is a conflict among those in the government seats about using this way of getting around an obligation that could very well follow should the strike be prolonged in the river ports to the point where the Maritime Employers Association might be forced to default in their undertakings to two of the principal banks that advanced them money, firstly for their retirement program two or three years ago and latterly for other reasons. I do not think we should let the bill go out of committee without some observation being made in this regard.
I find this proceeding distasteful. I abstained from voting for that reason, in part. Perhaps, more fundamentally, I abstained because this is the second time in the nine or ten years I have been here that this chamber has been caught up in determining the terms of settlement for a collective agreement between two parties. I am also somewhat disturbed about this proceeding, even though the difficulty has arisen in large measure because of abuse of the legal right to picket by striking employees albeit on

April 23, 1975

legal strike. I find no capacity within my thinking to tolerate or accept this, and I do not think any other member of the chamber does. I regret very much that the laws that now exist are not sufficient to correct this situation and that the government has used this thinly disguised pretext for bringing this measure before us. I regret that the existing authorities could not be invoked to protect the right of Quebec producers to have access to feed grains.
Based on the debate that we had a week ago tonight, I suspect that the urgency of this matter is not the national interest but that much narrower concern. Had we been dealing tonight with that much narrower concern, I would have felt a lot better as a member of this chamber. But we are not. We are here, as we all know, arbitrarily imposing upon employer and employee the terms of their collective agreement for the next two or three years. I regret this and I hope it will not be a precedent. I hope the minister's caution to the parties to the collective agreements will be taken at its face value and that this parliament does not intend lightly to find itself back in this position. The collective agreements with respect to the ILA and the Maritime Employers Association are ongoing in Saint John and will come up again in Halifax.
I hope that members of the unions involved, particularly the member companies of the Maritime Employers Association, do not sit too comfortably in their chairs tonight- I am not suggesting that they will do so-laughing at some of us because, in their opinion, they feel we have been dupes or pawns, unaware of some of the ramifications and implications of what lies behind the action of this parliament in ordering men back to work on the basis of a conciliation report.
I hope the minister will flex his muscles a bit and find some way to force parties to collective agreements to get on with the job of working out their problems. In my opinion, it was not good enough for the mediator in this case to meet with the parties once or twice and then wander off for three weeks. I am suspicious of that. I do not think we put our fullest effort into bringing the two sides together. The fact that they said they were not going to talk, and broke off discussions because of an apparent inability to get together, is all part of the adversary system. We may not like that, but we accept it. But it does not mean that the two sides cannot be brought together. In this case it is a matter of personal regret that a greater effort was not made so that we might have avoided doing what we are doing tonight.

expressed by a number of members to the effect that this is a distasteful business. I have listened many times to speeches in which people have said, "Let it not happen again"-but it seems to continue to happen. We felt very strongly, and acted accordingly in committee of the whole on the bill, that the compulsory part of this settlement should apply only to the wages and not to some of the other features of the Gold report, including those having to do with job security. To be specific, we think the House should have a chance to reconsider the narrowing of the compulsory element in the case of both groups, the longshoremen and the checkers and repairmen, and that in both cases we should reconsider the question of appointing an arbitrator. For this reason, we intend to move, as an amendment to third reading of the bill, that it be referred back to the committee of the whole House for the purpose of considering the subjects to which I have just referred.

Mr. Speaker, I shall only take a few minutes to ask the House, particularly my colleagues, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), to consider this third reading amendment on the basis of their argument and proposition. I say immediately that our amendment does not mean that there will be prolonged delay in the passage of this legislation. In fact, if the House accepts the amendment it means that we will revert to committee of the whole for five or ten minutes, accept the amendments we moved at the

committee stage, return to third reading and pass the kind of bill that my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver South and I suggested we should have so that we will not be legislatively arbitrating a settlement of the most contentious part of the dispute at these three ports, namely, job security. That is all our amendment is addressed to, and all we are asking the House to do now is reconsider what we failed to do in committee of the whole.
I reiterate that legislating that portion of the Gold report which is in very serious dispute can mean only that we will end up having even greater industrial strife at these three harbours in the months ahead. I hope I am wrong in this prediction, but from past experience in similar instances when we have dealt with legislation in the House in respect of industrial disputes and a settlement has been unfairly arrived at, it has lead to more industrial strife.
I agree with the hon. member for Calgary Centre that in respect of the amendment we are appointing an arbitrator to arbitrate part of the dispute in contention, but from what I have been informed and have read, the only really serious issue in contention is job security. I believe that most, if not all, of the other recommendations in Mr. Justice Gold's report are acceptable in whole or in part to both sides of the dispute, but job security is an issue which is of even more serious consequence than the issue of wages. I think both sides will accept, on the issue of wages, Mr. Justice Gold's recommendations.
If the House accepts this amendment, it will not mean there will be a prolonged delay of the legislation. We could still be out of here by ten o'clock. If we were to accept the amendment moved in committee of the whole, we would not be placing this parliament in the position of legislating a back to work law about which the hon. member for Vancouver South, the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East expressed fears, as I believe did the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert).
The issue to which I have referred is most contentious and could cause us serious difficulty in the months ahead. Let us take the matter of job security out of the legislation and put it in the hands of an arbitrator, whose decision would be binding in the same way as the decision of the arbitrator in the Vancouver situation. I admit this is only on that one issue, but it is the main issue and the one that caused this strike in the three ports. Surely it is not unreasonable to place this serious issue in the hands of an arbitrator rather than members of parliament legislating that kind of settlement.

Mr. Speaker, as I said in my statement this afternoon, I thought this bill was based essentially on a report submitted by the conciliation commissioner, Mr. Justice Gold, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and dated March 14, 1975. In a letter sent on the same day to the Minister of Labour, Mr. Gold wrote, among other things:
I regret to inform you that, although both sides tried their best during our almost daily meetings since I was appointed as conciliation commissioner, on December 24, 1974, they have not managed to reach an agreement. You will therefore find herewith my report and recommendations by way of a collective agreement draft.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe Mr. Justice Gold submitted that report to the Minister of Labour as the result of a very serious work; he himself reports: "Almost daily meetings". In other words, considerable attempts were made to reach an agreement, a conciliation, to sign a collective agreement which would satisfy both employers and employees. Unfortunately, after many meetings, they were unable to reach an agreement. And since March 14, the Minister of Labour let hold of events. We asked him questions in the House; we were concerned, and rightly so, about the effects of such unfortunate work stoppage, on behalf of workers and of those who suffer from this situation, in particular farming producers in the province of Quebec. More than a month later since today is April 23, the Government eventually decided to introduce a legislation, not of their own free will as the minister said, but because the parties of the dispute did not manage to reach an agreement even thanks to such a highly competent man as Mr. Justice Gold, who made every possible effort to try and reach an agreement acceptable to both parties.
This afternoon, a bill was introduced, Bill C-59. All the hon. members had the opportunity to give their opinion about the principle of the bill. Then, we studied it in committee of the whole. It is obvious that the bill pleases no one, at least not the hon. member for Bellechasse, but in view of the urgent need for a settlement, something has to be done in the interest of the public, and Parliament must legislate. I understand that NDP members have moved amendments with all their usual sincerity. I am convinced that these members wanted to take part in the debate and make, or at least suggest, amendments so that the bill would be more in keeping with the aspirations of the workers.
Since we have been in committee of the whole since the House resumed tonight at 8 p.m., and have made a clause by clause study of this bill, I believe that every effort has been made by Parliament to provide a measure as fair as possible to the workers and the employers. It is quite obvious that when we drive a car and must apply the brakes at a given time, the speed of the car is reduced. We reach our destination later, but this is sometimes necessary to avoid losing control in a detour. This is what we

Mr. Speaker, it is in this spirit that Parliament has made a serious study of this bill, and I hope that tonight we shall be able to go through the final stages of the bill in the House of Commons, even if we have to let the Senate do its own work later.
